name: Kingdom of Israel (Northern Kingdom)
summary: The northern polity that emerges after the division of the monarchy. Samaria becomes its capital under Omri; biblical and extra-biblical sources also use “Israel,” “Samaria,” and Assyrian dynastic labels in different contexts.

confidence.explanation: The historical polity is well attested, but its borders changed repeatedly. The plotted point is only a display anchor; territorial reconstructions are broad time-aware polygons.

locationNote: Display anchor near the central hill-country capital zone; not a capital coordinate or border claim.

name: Kingdom of Judah
summary: The southern kingdom centered on Jerusalem after the division of the monarchy. Its territorial reach varied significantly through the Iron Age.

confidence.explanation: Judah is historically well attested, but year-specific boundaries remain reconstructed. The point is a display anchor only.

locationNote: Display anchor at Jerusalem; use context polygons for generalized territorial orientation.

name: Aram-Damascus
summary: The Aramean kingdom centered on Damascus, a major rival and occasional ally of Israel before Assyrian annexation in the eighth century BCE.

confidence.explanation: The kingdom and its capital are historically secure; its changing frontiers are represented only as generalized context.

name: Neo-Assyrian Empire
summary: The imperial power that progressively intervened in Syria-Palestine, annexed Damascus and northern Israelite territories, ended the Northern Kingdom, and campaigned against Judah.

confidence.explanation: Assyria is abundantly attested; the point is a display anchor in its core, while imperial reach is visualized as broad context rather than a surveyed polygon.

name: Samaria / Sebaste
summary: Capital founded by Omri on a purchased hill and the political center of the Northern Kingdom until its Assyrian capture.

confidence.explanation: Ancient Samaria is securely identified at Sebastia. Archaeology illuminates royal/administrative occupation without labeling individual rooms as belonging to named kings.

historicalContext: Omri’s foundation shifted the northern capital from Tirzah to a defensible hill with strong regional connections. “Samaria” later becomes both a city name and a wider territorial designation.
archaeology: Excavations revealed major Iron Age architecture, administrative material, and ivories. Correlating particular buildings with Omri or Ahab depends on archaeological chronology rather than inscriptions naming rooms.

name: Tirzah / Tell el-Far‘ah (North)
summary: Early capital of the Northern Kingdom before Omri founded Samaria. Tell el-Far‘ah (North) is the leading identification.

confidence.explanation: The identification of Tirzah with Tell el-Far‘ah (North) is widely accepted but is best presented as probable rather than a label physically excavated from the site.

name: Jezreel / Tel Jezreel
summary: Royal center in the Jezreel Valley associated with Ahab, Jezebel, Naboth, and Jehu’s coup.

confidence.explanation: Tel Jezreel is securely identified with ancient Jezreel. The exact location of Naboth’s vineyard and individual palace spaces cannot be identified from the text.

archaeology: Excavated Iron Age fortifications and occupation provide royal-center context. They do not identify Naboth’s vineyard or the precise spot of Jehu’s encounter.

name: Mount Carmel
summary: The coastal mountain ridge that provides the setting for Elijah’s confrontation with the prophets of Baal in 1 Kings 18.

confidence.explanation: The Carmel range is geographically secure, but 1 Kings does not provide an archaeological coordinate for Elijah’s altar. The map uses a ridge-area anchor, not a claimed altar site.

locationNote: General Carmel ridge anchor. The later Muhraka tradition is not used as proof of the event site.

name: Brook Kerith / Cherith
summary: The brook or wadi east of the Jordan where Elijah is told to hide during the drought narrative.

confidence.explanation: The text gives a relative description east of the Jordan, but modern identifications are uncertain. No map pin is shown.

name: Zarephath / Sarepta
summary: Phoenician coastal town between Tyre and Sidon where Elijah stays with a widow during the drought.

confidence.explanation: Ancient Sarepta is securely localized near modern Sarafand on the Lebanese coast; the biblical household cannot be archaeologically singled out.

archaeology: Sarepta is an excavated Phoenician settlement with substantial Bronze/Iron Age remains, useful for cultural context rather than identification of the widow’s house.

name: Tishbe in Gilead
summary: Elijah is introduced as a Tishbite from Gilead. The exact settlement is not securely identified.

confidence.explanation: Several Transjordanian proposals exist, but no identification is sufficiently secure for a normal point.

name: Abel-meholah
summary: Home region of Elisha when Elijah calls him. Its exact location in the Jordan Valley is debated.

confidence.explanation: The biblical regional context is useful, but competing site proposals do not justify a precise coordinate.

name: Ramoth-gilead
summary: Strategic Transjordanian city repeatedly contested by Israel and Aram and the starting setting for Jehu’s coup.

confidence.explanation: The city’s regional setting in Gilead is clear, but proposed archaeological sites are disputed. It remains unpinned.

name: Aphek of the Aramean wars
summary: Aphek named in Ahab’s conflict with Ben-hadad. This is not automatically the same Aphek as the Philistine-camp site near the Yarkon.

confidence.explanation: Multiple places called Aphek existed. The 1 Kings 20 location is not securely identified, so the atlas creates a distinct unpinned record.

name: Jordan River
summary: The major river running from the Hula/Sea of Galilee system to the Dead Sea, repeatedly central to Elisha’s narratives.

confidence.explanation: The physical river is secure; individual miracle locations along it are not assigned exact coordinates.

locationNote: Display anchor on the river system; not the exact site of any individual event.

name: Kir-hareseth / Kir of Moab
summary: Moabite stronghold attacked in the coalition campaign of 2 Kings 3, commonly associated with the Kerak area.

confidence.explanation: The association with Kerak is longstanding and geographically plausible, but the precise equivalence is not epigraphically certain.

name: Qarqar / Tell Qarqur
summary: North Syrian battle location where Shalmaneser III fought a western coalition in 853 BCE. Tell Qarqur is the leading identification.

confidence.explanation: The battle is securely attested in Assyrian sources; identification of ancient Qarqar with Tell Qarqur is strong but presented as probable.

historicalContext: The Kurkh Monolith names Ahab of Israel among coalition participants. The battle is not narrated in Kings, so it is shown as extra-biblical historical context.

name: Tekoa / Khirbet Tuqu‘
summary: Judean hill-country town associated with the prophet Amos.

confidence.explanation: The ancient town is commonly identified with the ruins near modern Tuquʿ. The atlas uses the site as a probable anchor, not an exact residence of Amos.

name: Moresheth-gath
summary: Shephelah town associated with the prophet Micah. Proposed identifications exist, but the exact site remains uncertain.

confidence.explanation: Moresheth belongs in the Judah/Philistia borderland setting, but a precise modern identification is not secure enough for a pin.

name: Joppa / Jaffa
summary: Ancient Mediterranean port from which Jonah boards a ship bound for Tarshish in the narrative.

confidence.explanation: Ancient Joppa is securely located at modern Jaffa/Tel Yafo. The route to Tarshish remains unknown because Tarshish itself is disputed.

name: Tarshish
summary: Distant maritime destination named in Jonah 1. Its identification is disputed and should not be reduced to a single point such as Tartessos without qualification.

confidence.explanation: Several locations have been proposed across the Mediterranean and beyond. The atlas leaves Tarshish unpinned.

interpretations.title: Western Mediterranean / Tartessos family of proposals
interpretations.summary: A long-standing proposal associates Tarshish with the far western Mediterranean, sometimes Tartessos in Iberia; the identification is not certain.

interpretations.title: Tarshish as a broader maritime/distant-land term in some contexts
interpretations.summary: Biblical uses of Tarshish and “ships of Tarshish” complicate a single-location model; not every occurrence necessarily functions identically.

name: Mediterranean Sea
summary: The Mediterranean maritime world connecting Phoenicia, Philistia, Joppa, Egypt, Anatolia, Cyprus, and the wider ancient world.

confidence.explanation: The sea is physically established; the coordinate is only a display anchor for broad maritime context.

name: Nineveh
summary: Major Assyrian city on the Tigris opposite modern Mosul; later imperial capital and the destination of Jonah’s commission.

confidence.explanation: Nineveh is securely identified archaeologically. The historicity and literary dating of the Jonah narrative are separate interpretive questions.

archaeology: Extensive Assyrian palaces, walls, inscriptions, and relief programs are known. These establish the imperial city, not the specific events narrated in Jonah.

name: Kalhu / Calah / Nimrud
summary: Major Neo-Assyrian royal city south of Nineveh, associated with imperial administration and monuments such as the Black Obelisk.

confidence.explanation: The Assyrian city Kalhu is securely identified with Nimrud.

name: Dur-Sharrukin / Khorsabad
summary: Royal city founded by Sargon II near Nineveh, relevant to the imperial context following the fall of Samaria.

confidence.explanation: Dur-Sharrukin is securely identified with Khorsabad.

name: Gozan / Guzana / Tell Halaf
summary: Upper Mesopotamian city and region named among destinations of deported Israelites after the fall of Samaria.

confidence.explanation: Biblical Gozan is securely associated with Guzana/Tell Halaf in the Khabur region.

name: Habor / Khabur River
summary: Euphrates tributary region named in the Assyrian deportation notices.

confidence.explanation: The Khabur river system is securely identified. The biblical phrase “Habor, the river of Gozan” does not specify an individual deportee settlement.

name: Halah
summary: One of the locations named in the Assyrian deportation formula for the Northern Kingdom. Its precise identification remains uncertain.

confidence.explanation: Scholarly proposals exist, but the atlas does not assign Halah a synthetic coordinate.

name: Media
summary: Broad Iranian highland region whose cities are named among Assyrian deportation destinations in Kings.

confidence.explanation: Media is a known historical region, but Kings does not name the specific Median cities. The point is only a broad display anchor.

name: Lachish / Tel Lachish
summary: Major fortified city of Judah captured by Sennacherib in 701 BCE and vividly represented in Assyrian palace reliefs.

confidence.explanation: Tel Lachish is securely identified; the Assyrian destruction horizon and siege works provide unusually strong archaeological-historical correlation for 701 BCE.

archaeology: Excavations exposed the Assyrian siege ramp, defenses, destruction deposits, and mass evidence of the 701 BCE assault. Sennacherib’s Lachish reliefs independently depict the siege.

name: Libnah (Judah)
summary: Judean town mentioned when the Assyrian field commander leaves Lachish in the 701 BCE campaign narrative. Its precise archaeological identification remains debated.

confidence.explanation: Several Shephelah sites have been proposed. The atlas leaves Libnah unpinned rather than choosing one candidate.

name: Siloam Tunnel / Hezekiah’s Tunnel
summary: Rock-cut water tunnel carrying Gihon Spring water toward the southern part of ancient Jerusalem, commonly associated with Hezekiah’s preparations.

confidence.explanation: The tunnel itself is an established archaeological feature. Its connection with Hezekiah is widely accepted from combined archaeological and textual context, but the tunnel inscription does not name a king.

archaeology: The Siloam Inscription records the meeting of two tunneling crews. Dating and the exact sequence of Jerusalem’s Iron Age water systems require archaeological analysis beyond the biblical attribution.

name: Conduit of the Upper Pool / Fuller’s Field road
summary: Jerusalem topographic reference in Isaiah’s encounter with Ahaz and later in the Assyrian envoy narrative.

confidence.explanation: The biblical relative topography is important, but the exact Iron Age “Upper Pool” and Fuller’s Field road are not securely identified enough for a point.
